nodes.label: The pagan Roman province
nodes.full: Roman Egypt before Constantine — a still-largely-pagan province with functioning temples, a Museum, and the beginnings of a persecuted church. This folio is the story of that Egypt becoming Christian and Coptic.
nodes.src: background — see the folio egypt-30bc-300ad (Roman Egypt)

nodes.label: Constantinople and the Empire
nodes.full: The Christian Roman empire ruled from Constantinople, whose grain came from Egypt, whose emperors imposed church councils on it, and whose army defended it — until it could not.
nodes.src: background — added on review; A.H.M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964)

nodes.label: The Sasanian Empire
nodes.full: Khosrow II's Persia overran the Roman east, held Egypt for a decade (619–629), and was then destroyed by Heraclius — a mutual exhaustion that opened the way for the Arab conquest.
nodes.src: background — added on review; Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)

nodes.label: The Caliphate and Islam
nodes.full: The Rashidun and then Umayyad caliphate that took Egypt in 641 and ruled it from the new city of Fustat, opening the long transformation to a Muslim, Arabic-speaking country.
nodes.src: background — added on review; belongs to the next folio; Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

nodes.label: Constantine and the Christian turn
nodes.full: Under Constantine, Christianity went from persecuted to favoured. The toleration of 313 was followed by imperial patronage of the church; Constantine summoned the Council of Nicaea in 325 to settle the Arian dispute that began in Alexandria; and from 330 the grain that had fed Rome for three centuries was redirected to feed his new capital, Constantinople. The province was reordered again, and its bishop of Alexandria began to matter to emperors.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Life of Constantine, Historia Ecclesiastica 10. The grain to Constantinople: the Theodosian Code and Justinian's Edict 13. Roger Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993) pp.1–20, 285–89.

nodes.label: The Augustal Prefecture and the diocese of Egypt
nodes.full: Diocletian's and Constantine's reforms broke Egypt into a set of small provinces — Aegyptus, Augustamnica, Arcadia, the Thebaid, the Libyas — grouped as a diocese under the praefectus Augustalis at Alexandria, with civil government separated from military command and a dux for frontier defence. Justinian's edict of 539 partly reversed this, recombining civil and military power in each province's governor to make the machine work. The apparatus stayed recognisably Roman down to the Arab conquest.
nodes.src: Justinian, Edict 13 (539). The provincial structure: Bernhard Palme, 'The Imperial Presence: Government and Army', in R.S. Bagnall (ed.), Egypt in the Byzantine World (2007); J.G. Keenan and the papyri of the office.

nodes.label: Julian and the pagan last stand
nodes.full: The emperor Julian tried to roll the empire back to the old gods, reopening temples and restoring sacrifice. In Alexandria the news let a mob seize and lynch the deeply unpopular Arian bishop George of Cappadocia and two officials, burning the bodies and scattering the ashes 'so no shrine could be raised'. Julian merely reprimanded the city. His death on campaign in Persia two years later ended the reaction; no emperor after him favoured paganism.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 22.11; Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 3.2–3; Julian, Letter 21 (to the Alexandrians). Christopher Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997) pp.280–95.

nodes.label: Theodosius I outlaws the old gods
nodes.full: Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the empire's only lawful religion and, in a series of edicts culminating in 391–392, banned all sacrifice and closed the temples. In Alexandria that same year the patriarch Theophilus led the demolition of the Serapeum. When Theodosius died in 395 the empire was permanently divided, and Egypt, with its grain and its turbulent church, belonged to the eastern half ruled from Constantinople.
nodes.src: Theodosian Code 16.10.10–12. The Serapeum: Rufinus, Historia Ecclesiastica 11.22–30; Socrates 5.16–17. Garth Fowden, 'Bishops and Temples in the Eastern Roman Empire', JTS 29 (1978).

nodes.label: Marcian, Chalcedon and the killing of Proterius
nodes.full: The emperor Marcian convened the Council of Chalcedon in 451, whose definition of Christ 'in two natures' Egypt overwhelmingly rejected. When the imperial candidate Proterius was installed as patriarch of Alexandria under military guard, the city seethed; on Marcian's death in 457 a mob seized Proterius in the baptistery, killed him, dragged the body through the streets and burned it. From then on the imperial and the Egyptian churches were at war.
nodes.src: Evagrius, Historia Ecclesiastica 2.5, 2.8; Zachariah of Mytilene 3.11–4.1. W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972) pp.148–83.

nodes.label: Justinian and Egypt
nodes.full: Justinian's wars of reconquest ran on Egyptian grain and taxes. He reorganised the province's government by the edict of 539, closed the temple of Isis at Philae around 537 — the last functioning temple of the old Egyptian religion — and sent missionaries who converted the Nubian kingdom of Nobadia. His wife Theodora shielded the persecuted Miaphysite leaders, and the plague of 541, which reached the empire through the Egyptian port of Pelusium, killed a large share of the population.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1.19 (Philae), Secret History; John of Ephesus. Justinian's Edict 13. Plague: Procopius, Wars 2.22–23; Peter Sarris, 'The Justinianic Plague', Continuity and Change 17 (2002).

nodes.label: Heraclius — Egypt lost and lost again
nodes.full: Heraclius rose to power on a revolt launched from Roman Africa and Egypt against the tyrant Phocas. He then lost Egypt to Persia for a decade (619–629), recovered it by treaty, and tried to reunite the fractured church with a compromise formula, Monotheletism, enforced in Egypt by the patriarch and governor Cyrus 'the Caucasian' with a persecution the Coptic sources call the worst they had known. It left Egypt bitterly divided and militarily hollow when the Arab armies arrived at the end of his reign.
nodes.src: Nicephorus, Short History; the Chronicle of John of Nikiou. Walter Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium (2003) and Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992).

nodes.label: Athanasius — bishop against the world
nodes.full: Athanasius held the see of Alexandria for 45 turbulent years, defending the Nicene doctrine that the Son is fully God against the Arian party favoured by a run of emperors. He was deposed and exiled five times, twice fleeing to the desert monks whose cause he championed and whose founder he memorialised in the Life of Antony. He built the patriarchate into a power that emperors had to reckon with and bound it permanently to the monastic movement.
nodes.src: Athanasius, Orations against the Arians, Life of Antony, Festal Letters, Apology to Constantius. Timothy Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993); David Brakke, Athanasius and the Politics of Asceticism (1995).

nodes.label: Theophilus — the temple-breaker
nodes.full: Theophilus turned the patriarchate into a machine of Christianisation and church politics. He led the destruction of the Serapeum in 391 and the conversion of pagan sites into churches, then reversed his own theology to purge the Origenist monks of Nitria (the 'Tall Brothers'), whose flight to Constantinople helped bring down John Chrysostom. Ruthless and effective, he handed a dominant see to his nephew and pupil Cyril.
nodes.src: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 6.7; Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom. Norman Russell, Theophilus of Alexandria (2007).

nodes.label: Cyril of Alexandria — the arbiter of orthodoxy
nodes.full: Cyril, Theophilus's nephew, was the age's most formidable theologian of the Incarnation — his formula for the unity of Christ shaped every later council — and its most aggressive churchman. Early in his tenure he expelled the Jewish community of Alexandria and clashed with the prefect Orestes in the poisoned atmosphere that led to Hypatia's murder in 415. In 431 he dominated the Council of Ephesus, had his rival Nestorius condemned in absentia, and made Alexandria the judge of what counted as orthodox.
nodes.src: Cyril, On the Unity of Christ, Twelve Anathemas, Letters. Socrates 7.7, 7.13–15. Susan Wessel, Cyril of Alexandria and the Nestorian Controversy (2004); John McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria (1994).

nodes.label: Dioscorus and the Chalcedonian rupture
nodes.full: Cyril's successor Dioscorus pushed Alexandrian dominance too far: at a council at Ephesus in 449, backed by imperial troops and monks, he rehabilitated the extreme Eutyches and had his opponents beaten — a session the pope called a 'robbery'. Two years later the Council of Chalcedon reversed it, defined Christ 'in two natures', and deposed and exiled Dioscorus. The Egyptian church refused to accept either his deposition or the definition, and the split became permanent.
nodes.src: Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (Richard Price & Michael Gaddis translation, 2005). W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972) pp.1–49.

nodes.label: The two patriarchs of Alexandria
nodes.full: After Chalcedon, Alexandria usually had two rival patriarchs: an anti-Chalcedonian (Miaphysite) one recognised by the great majority of Egyptian Christians, and a Chalcedonian one — nicknamed 'Melkite', the king's man — installed and protected by the imperial garrison, often unable to move freely in his own city. The theologian Severus of Antioch took refuge in the Egyptian desert; Coptic and Melkite churches, calendars and monasteries ran in parallel for nearly two centuries.
nodes.src: Zachariah of Mytilene; the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria. Ewa Wipszycka, The Alexandrian Church: People and Institutions (2015); Frend (1972) pp.143–295.

nodes.label: Benjamin I — the Coptic Church survives the conquest
nodes.full: Benjamin I became Coptic patriarch just before the Persians came, fled the Byzantine Monothelete persecution under Cyrus, and spent thirteen years in hiding among the monasteries of the Thebaid. After the Arab conquest the general 'Amr ibn al-'As, told the true head of the Egyptian church was in exile, sent him a safe-conduct; Benjamin returned to Alexandria in 644, recovered the churches the Melkites had held, and re-established the Coptic hierarchy that has continued unbroken since.
nodes.src: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria (the 'Life of Benjamin' by his contemporary); John of Nikiou, ch.120–21. C. Detlef G. Müller, and Phil Booth, 'The Last Years of Cyrus, Patriarch of Alexandria', Travaux et Mémoires 20/1 (2016).

nodes.label: The Persian occupation of Egypt
nodes.full: In 619 the army of Khosrow II under the general Shahrbaraz overran Egypt, taking Alexandria after a siege, and ended seven centuries of unbroken Roman rule. For a decade Egypt was a Sasanian province, its administration continuing in Greek and Coptic under Persian oversight, its grain no longer sailing to Constantinople — a loss that helped push the eastern empire to the brink. Heraclius's victories over Persia forced the army's withdrawal by treaty in 629.
nodes.src: The Persian-period papyri (Greek, Coptic and a few Middle Persian): Bernhard Palme and others. Chronicle of John of Nikiou. James Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010).

nodes.label: The Arab conquest of Egypt
nodes.full: 'Amr ibn al-'As entered Egypt from Palestine in December 639 with a few thousand men, took Pelusium, beat the Byzantine field army at Heliopolis in July 640, and after a seven-month siege forced the surrender of the great fortress of Babylon in April 641. Alexandria, defended but demoralised and led by the compromised governor-patriarch Cyrus, was handed over by treaty; the last Byzantine troops sailed in September 642. A naval attempt to retake the city in 645 failed.
nodes.src: Chronicle of John of Nikiou (ch.111–21); al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr. Alfred J. Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902; 2nd ed. 1978); Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007) pp.144–68.

nodes.label: 'Amr ibn al-'As and the founding of Fustat
nodes.full: 'Amr governed the new province from a garrison town, Fustat, laid out around his army's camp beside the fortress of Babylon — the settlement that would grow into Cairo — where he built the first mosque in Africa. The bulk of the population kept its Coptic church and paid a land-and-poll tax (kharaj and jizya); the Greek-speaking Byzantine elite largely left. Egyptian grain was again shipped east, now to Medina, along a re-dug Red Sea canal.
nodes.src: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr. The bilingual Greek–Arabic papyri of the conquest generation (PERF 558, the earliest dated Arabic document, 643). Petra Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State (2013); Wladimir Kubiak, Al-Fustat: Its Foundation and Early Urban Development (1987).

nodes.label: The destruction of the Serapeum
nodes.full: After Theodosius's edicts banned the temple cults, a confrontation in Alexandria escalated into a siege of the Serapeum by pagans who had seized Christian hostages. When an imperial rescript pardoned the pagans but ordered the temple destroyed, the patriarch Theophilus led a crowd that tore down the colossal statue of Serapis and demolished the sanctuary and its library. Nothing else so clearly marked the end of the old religion in its greatest stronghold.
nodes.src: Rufinus, Historia Ecclesiastica 11.22–30; Sozomen 7.15; Eunapius, Lives of the Sophists (a hostile pagan account). Johannes Hahn, Gewalt und religiöser Konflikt (2004).

nodes.label: The murder of Hypatia
nodes.full: Hypatia, head of the Neoplatonist school of Alexandria and a respected mathematician and astronomer, was a friend and adviser of the imperial prefect Orestes, then locked in a power struggle with the patriarch Cyril. A rumour that she was the obstacle to their reconciliation led a mob, including church attendants called parabalani, to drag her from her carriage into a church, kill her, and burn the body. The killing shocked contemporaries and has stood ever since as the symbol of faith turned murderous.
nodes.src: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 7.15; the Suda; John of Nikiou 84 (a hostile version). Maria Dzielska, Hypatia of Alexandria (1995); Edward Watts, Hypatia (2017).

nodes.label: The street wars of Christian Alexandria
nodes.full: For over a century, control of the see of Alexandria was fought in the streets. Disputed elections brought riots; bishops installed by emperors were besieged in their churches or lynched (George in 361, Proterius in 457); rival congregations, the church strongmen known as parabalani, and imperial troops all played a part. The city's habit of settling religious questions by force — inherited from its Greek–Jewish–pagan quarrels — made it ungovernable on any other terms.
nodes.src: Athanasius, History of the Arians; Socrates and Sozomen, passim. Christopher Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997); Ewa Wipszycka on the parabalani.

nodes.label: The raids of the Blemmyes and Nobades
nodes.full: With Rome's frontier pulled back to Aswan, the desert peoples the sources call Blemmyes and Nobades raided Upper Egypt and the Western oases, plundering monasteries and towns and reaching Philae, where the Blemmyes still worshipped Isis and periodically borrowed her statue. A treaty negotiated by the general Maximinus in 452 bought a hundred-year peace, and over the following century missionaries drew both peoples into Christianity.
nodes.src: Priscus of Panium, fragments; Procopius, Wars 1.19. László Török, Between Two Worlds (2009) pp.515–26; the Blemmyan documents from Gebelein.

nodes.label: Enforcing Chalcedon by force
nodes.full: For 85 years the empire tried to make Egypt accept the Council of Chalcedon, and Egypt would not. The imperial patriarch Proterius was murdered by the crowd in 457; anti-Chalcedonian patriarchs were exiled again and again; troops were sent against Alexandrian congregations; a formula of compromise, the Henotikon of 482, satisfied no one; and Justinian finally deposed the last non-Chalcedonian patriarch, Theodosius, in 536. The result was not conformity but a settled, self-conscious separate Egyptian church.
nodes.src: Evagrius, Historia Ecclesiastica 2–4; Zachariah of Mytilene. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972); Volker Menze, Justinian and the Making of the Syrian Orthodox Church (2008).

nodes.label: Egypt and the fall of Phocas
nodes.full: When the exarch of Africa raised a revolt against the emperor Phocas, he sent his nephew Nicetas to take Egypt while his son Heraclius sailed for Constantinople. Nicetas defeated Phocas's general Bonosus in hard fighting around Alexandria and secured the province — and with it the grain supply and a treasury — for the rebellion that made Heraclius emperor. It showed again that whoever held Egypt could make an emperor.
nodes.src: Chronicle of John of Nikiou 107–10; Nicephorus, Short History 1–2. Walter Kaegi, Heraclius (2003) pp.37–48.

nodes.label: The Persian conquest of Egypt
nodes.full: The Sasanian general Shahrbaraz, having taken Syria and Palestine, invaded Egypt in 617–618 and captured Alexandria in 619 after a siege — reportedly betrayed through an unguarded canal culvert. It was the first time in nearly 950 years, since Alexander, that Egypt had passed out of Greek or Roman hands, and for the eastern empire the loss of its grain and revenue was close to fatal.
nodes.src: Chronicle of John of Nikiou 109–10; the Khuzistan Chronicle; the Life of Anastasius the Persian. Clive Foss, 'The Persians in the Roman Near East', JRAS 13 (2003).

nodes.label: Heliopolis and the siege of Babylon
nodes.full: 'Amr ibn al-'As, reinforced to perhaps 15,000 men, defeated the Byzantine field army under Theodore at Heliopolis in July 640, scattering the garrison of the Delta. He then laid siege to the fortress of Babylon at the head of the Delta, the key to Egypt; after seven months and the failure of relief, and with the governor Cyrus negotiating behind the walls, it surrendered on 9 April 641. The road to Alexandria lay open.
nodes.src: John of Nikiou 111–17; al-Baladhuri; Ibn Abd al-Hakam. Alfred Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902) pp.234–320; Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007).

nodes.label: The fall of Alexandria
nodes.full: The patriarch-governor Cyrus, sent back from exile to make terms, signed a treaty with 'Amr on 8 November 641: an eleven-month truce, payment of tribute, and the peaceful evacuation of the Byzantine forces. Alexandria — walled, garrisoned and reachable by sea, and in no military sense beaten — was handed over on 17 September 642. A Byzantine fleet retook it briefly in 645; 'Amr recovered it, and Roman rule in Egypt was finished for good.
nodes.src: The 'Treaty of Alexandria': John of Nikiou 120; al-Tabari. Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902) pp.320–68; Phil Booth, 'The Muslim Conquest of Egypt Reconsidered', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013).

nodes.label: The late-antique provincial state
nodes.full: The Roman machine kept running, reformed. Egypt was a diocese of small provinces under the Augustal prefect, with civil and military commands divided, sprawling bureaus (officia), and a tax system shifting from grain toward gold assessed on a fixed multi-year cycle. But the curial class that had run the towns was collapsing under the fiscal burden, and its functions drifted toward bishops, great landowners and appointed strongmen — the state present everywhere on paper, thin on the ground.
nodes.src: Roger Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993) pp.54–92, 153–71; Bernhard Palme in Bagnall (ed.), Egypt in the Byzantine World (2007). Tax in gold: A.H.M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964).

nodes.label: The great estate — the house of Apion
nodes.full: The archive of the Apion family, senators and consuls who owned vast estates around Oxyrhynchus, is the most detailed picture of a landholding operation to survive from antiquity: thousands of documents recording rents in kind and cash, granaries and wine presses, irrigation machinery, a payroll of tenants, guards and craftsmen, a private prison, and a private armed retinue. The house also collected the public taxes of its district and delivered them to the state — a fusion of private wealth and public function.
nodes.src: The Oxyrhynchus Apion papyri: E.R. Hardy, The Large Estates of Byzantine Egypt (1931); Todd Hickey, Wine, Wealth, and the State in Late Antique Egypt: The House of Apion at Oxyrhynchus (2012); Peter Sarris, Economy and Society in the Age of Justinian (2006).

nodes.label: The pagarch and the retreat of the salaried state
nodes.full: By the sixth century a district was often run by a pagarch — in practice a great local landowner given responsibility for its taxes and public order, holding an office that shaded into a private lordship. Villages complained bitterly of pagarchs who over-assessed, quartered troops, and jailed defaulters. The state increasingly governed the countryside not through its own officials but by delegating to whoever was already powerful there, a pattern that would carry straight through the Arab conquest.
nodes.src: J.G. Keenan, 'The Aphrodite Papyri and Village Life in Byzantine Egypt', Bulletin de la Société d'Archéologie Copte 26 (1984); the petitions of Dioscorus of Aphrodito against the pagarch. Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993) pp.161–65.

nodes.label: The church as an arm of government
nodes.full: The Christian church became a public institution. A bishop's court had legal standing; the church was, after the state and the great houses, the largest landowner in Egypt; and it ran the welfare the classical city never had — grain doles, hospitals, orphanages, the ransoming of captives, hostels for travellers. The bishop was often the effective 'father of the city', negotiating with governors, tax officials and, in the end, conquerors.
nodes.src: Ewa Wipszycka, Les ressources et les activités économiques des églises en Égypte (1972) and The Alexandrian Church (2015). Peter Brown, Poverty and Leadership in the Later Roman Empire (2002).

nodes.label: Roman codes and Coptic contracts
nodes.full: The formal law was the Theodosian Code of 438 and Justinian's Corpus of 534, administered in Greek by imperial judges. But in the villages a growing share of everyday business — sales, leases, loans, marriage settlements, wills, dispute settlements — was written in Coptic, with its own set formulae, before local scribes, priests or monastic notaries. A distinct provincial legal practice, part Roman and part Egyptian, ran under the imperial one and outlasted it.
nodes.src: Coptic legal documents: Artur Steinwenter, Das Recht der koptischen Urkunden (1955); Leslie MacCoull, Coptic Legal Documents (2009). The Greek framework: Joseph Mélèze Modrzejewski.

nodes.label: The village of Aphrodito and its notary
nodes.full: The Upper Egyptian village of Aphrodito held the rare privilege of paying its taxes directly to the state rather than through a pagarch, and fought to keep it. Its records survive largely through Dioscorus, a landowner, lawyer, notary and Greek poet who drafted the village's contracts and petitions and represented it at Constantinople. His archive is the fullest view anywhere of how an ordinary late-Roman village actually worked — its land, its church, its feuds, its dealings with the powerful.
nodes.src: The Dioscorus archive: Jean-Luc Fournet (ed.), Les archives de Dioscore d'Aphrodité cent ans après leur découverte (2008); Leslie MacCoull, Dioscorus of Aphrodito: His Work and His World (1988).

nodes.label: The frontier army and its collapse
nodes.full: Late Roman Egypt was held by a field army near Alexandria and a screen of frontier troops (limitanei) in fortified Nile towns, backed by federate arrangements paying the Nobades and Blemmyes to keep the peace. It was enough for raiders and internal disorder but had hollowed out by the seventh century: the Persians overran the country in two years, and 'Amr ibn al-'As conquered it with a force that at its largest numbered perhaps fifteen thousand men.
nodes.src: The Notitia Dignitatum (Or. 28, 31). Bernhard Palme, 'The Imperial Presence', in Bagnall (ed.), Egypt in the Byzantine World (2007); Constantin Zuckerman, Du village à l'empire (2004) on the Thebaid garrison.

nodes.label: The end of the temples
nodes.full: Across the fourth to sixth centuries the temples of Egypt were closed, converted to churches, quarried, or simply left to the sand as their endowments were confiscated and their priesthoods dispersed. The last hieroglyphic inscription was cut at Philae in 394, the last text in Demotic there in 452, and around 537 Justinian's officers shut the Isis temple of Philae itself — the final working sanctuary of a religion three and a half thousand years old.
nodes.src: Last hieroglyphic and Demotic graffiti at Philae: the 'Esmet-Akhom' inscription (394) and the 452 text. Procopius, Wars 1.19.36–37. Jitse Dijkstra, Philae and the End of Ancient Egyptian Religion (2008); David Frankfurter, Religion in Roman Egypt (1998).

nodes.label: The Arian and Christological wars
nodes.full: Alexandria was where the empire's great doctrinal fights began. The priest Arius' teaching that the Son was a created being provoked the Council of Nicaea in 325, which defined him as 'of one being' with the Father — a formula Athanasius spent his life defending against Arian emperors. A century later the question shifted to how godhead and manhood met in Christ: Cyril of Alexandria's insistence on their unity, against Nestorius, carried the Council of Ephesus in 431 and made Alexandrian theology the standard of orthodoxy.
nodes.src: Athanasius, Orations against the Arians. Acts of Nicaea and Ephesus. R.P.C. Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988); John McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria and the Christological Controversy (1994).

nodes.label: Chalcedon and the birth of the Coptic Church
nodes.full: The Council of Chalcedon in 451 defined Christ as existing 'in two natures', divine and human. Egypt read this as a betrayal of Cyril and a concession to Nestorius, and held instead to 'one incarnate nature' of the Word — Miaphysitism. Despite eighty-five years of imperial pressure, the Egyptian church refused to conform, and became a distinct communion, increasingly identified with the Coptic language and a sense of Egyptian religious nationhood: the Coptic Orthodox Church, still separate today.
nodes.src: Acts of Chalcedon (Price & Gaddis, 2005). W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972); Aziz Atiya, A History of Eastern Christianity (1968); Stephen Davis, The Early Coptic Papacy (2004).

nodes.label: Antony and the birth of the desert life
nodes.full: Around 270 a young Egyptian named Antony gave away his land and withdrew, first to the edge of his village and then deep into the Eastern Desert, to seek God in solitude and struggle with demons. Athanasius' Life of Antony, written soon after his death, became one of the most widely read books of late antiquity and the template for the ascetic vocation. Thousands followed him into the deserts of Egypt — 'the desert was made a city', in a famous phrase.
nodes.src: Athanasius, Life of Antony (Greek text; the earlier Coptic tradition). Samuel Rubenson, The Letters of St. Antony (1995); David Brakke, Demons and the Making of the Monk (2006).

nodes.label: Pachomius and the invention of the monastery
nodes.full: Where Antony's followers lived alone, Pachomius gathered his in a walled community at Tabennesi around 320, with a written Rule governing common prayer, common meals, assigned work, dress and the day's hours, under an abbot. By his death he headed a federation of nine monasteries and two nunneries with thousands of members. This cenobitic model — the organised, rule-bound monastery — is Egypt's, and it became the standard form of monastic life across the entire Christian world.
nodes.src: The Pachomian Koinonia (Armand Veilleux's translation, 1980–82): the Lives, the Rule, the letters. James Goehring, Ascetics, Society, and the Desert (1999); Philip Rousseau, Pachomius (1985).

nodes.label: The monastic desert and its export
nodes.full: The monastic settlements of the Wadi Natrun and the Nile-Delta desert — Nitria, the 'Cells' of Kellia, Scetis — became the spiritual capital of Christendom. Their teaching survives as the Apophthegmata, the terse Sayings of the Desert Fathers; Evagrius Ponticus turned it into a system of the spiritual life; and a stream of visitors — Palladius, John Cassian, the authors of the Historia Monachorum — carried Egyptian monastic practice to Palestine, Constantinople, Gaul and eventually the Latin west.
nodes.src: The Apophthegmata Patrum: Benedicta Ward's translation (1975). Historia Monachorum in Aegypto; Palladius, Lausiac History; John Cassian, Institutes and Conferences. Hugh Evelyn White, The Monasteries of the Wâdi 'n Natrûn (1926–33).

nodes.label: Shenoute and the White Monastery
nodes.full: Shenoute of Atripe ruled the White Monastery near Sohag for some eight decades, a federation of several thousand monks and nuns held to a fierce discipline. He led armed raids on the temples and estates of the region's surviving pagan landowners, fed refugees from Blemmyan raids by the thousand, browbeat governors, and left an enormous body of sermons, rules and letters — the greatest achievement of literary Coptic and the model of the powerful Egyptian abbot.
nodes.src: Shenoute's corpus: Stephen Emmel, Shenoute's Literary Corpus (2004); the ongoing editions. Ariel López, Shenoute of Atripe and the Uses of Poverty (2013); Rebecca Krawiec, Shenoute and the Women of the White Monastery (2002).

nodes.label: The shrines of the saints and martyrs
nodes.full: Christian Egypt replaced the temple oracle with the saint's tomb. The greatest shrine was Abu Mina, west of Alexandria, built over the grave of the soldier-martyr Menas: a pilgrimage city with a basilica, baths and hostels, whose little terracotta flasks stamped with the saint between two camels have been dug up from Britain to the Sudan. The dead were healed by sleeping at such shrines, the martyrs' acts were the popular reading, and the calendar itself began from the 'Era of the Martyrs'.
nodes.src: Abu Mina: Peter Grossmann, Abu Mina I: Die Gruftkirche und die Gruft (1989). Menas ampullae: Zsolt Kiss and others. Arietta Papaconstantinou, Le culte des saints en Égypte des Byzantins aux Abbassides (2001).

nodes.label: Literary Coptic and the monastic library
nodes.full: Coptic — Egyptian written in Greek letters — grew from a device for glossing spells and translating scripture into a full literary language. Shenoute's sermons and rules are its high point; around them stand hymns, saints' lives, monastic letters, homilies and apocrypha, standardised in the Sahidic dialect of the south. The monasteries were its centres of production: the White Monastery library alone held thousands of volumes, now scattered across the world's collections, of theology, exegesis, and practical handbooks.
nodes.src: Tito Orlandi, 'Coptic Literature', in Pearson & Goehring (eds.), The Roots of Egyptian Christianity (1986). Stephen Emmel, Shenoute's Literary Corpus (2004). The White Monastery library: the reconstruction project of Emmel and others.

nodes.label: Coptic art and the textiles
nodes.full: Late-antique Egyptian Christian art has an unmistakable look: chunky, frontal limestone sculpture for niches and tombstones, the old life-sign ankh redrawn as the looped cross, and above all the textiles — tapestry-woven roundels and bands on linen tunics and hangings, mixing dancing maenads and hunting scenes with crosses, saints and the Virgin. Preserved by the thousand in the dry cemeteries of Akhmim and Antinoopolis, 'Coptic textiles' are the largest surviving body of ancient woven art.
nodes.src: Cäcilia Fluck & Gisela Helmecke (eds.), Egypt's Sunken Treasures and the Coptic textile literature; Marie-Hélène Rutschowscaya, Coptic Fabrics (1990). Sculpture: Klaus Wessel, Coptic Art (1965); Thelma Thomas, Late Antique Egyptian Funerary Sculpture (2000).

nodes.label: The church and the painted monastery
nodes.full: Christian Egypt covered the country in basilicas — the pilgrim city of Abu Mina, the huge churches of Hermopolis and the Fayum, the fortress-like Red and White Monasteries with their re-used pharaonic blocks. Monastic chapels and cells at Bawit and Saqqara were painted with Christ enthroned in glory above the Virgin and apostles, ranks of local monk-saints, and biblical scenes, in a bold, flat, brightly coloured style that is one of the roots of later icon painting.
nodes.src: Peter Grossmann, Christliche Architektur in Ägypten (2002). Bawit: Jean Clédat, Le monastère et la nécropole de Baouît (1904–16); Saqqara (Apa Jeremiah): J.E. Quibell, Excavations at Saqqara (1907–12).

nodes.label: The last Greek poets of Egypt
nodes.full: Egypt produced the last great Greek poetry of antiquity. Nonnus of Panopolis wrote the sprawling 48-book Dionysiaca and, in the same dense style, a hexameter paraphrase of John's Gospel; a whole 'school' of Panopolitan and other Egyptian poets — Cyrus, Christodorus, Colluthus, Musaeus — carried classical epic and epigram into the sixth century, some as travelling performers hawking encomia to officials. Dioscorus of Aphrodito's ambitious, half-successful verse petitions show the tradition reaching down to a village notary.
nodes.src: Alan Cameron, 'Wandering Poets: A Literary Movement in Byzantine Egypt', Historia 14 (1965). Nonnus: the Budé edition. Laura Miguélez-Cavero, Poems in Context: Greek Poetry in the Egyptian Thebaid 200–600 AD (2008).

nodes.label: The codex and the bound book
nodes.full: Egypt is where the ancient book changed shape. Through late antiquity the papyrus roll gave way to the codex — folded sheets sewn between covers — and Christians adopted the new form early and almost exclusively. The thirteen leather-bound Gnostic codices buried near Nag Hammadi around 350, with their cartonnage-stiffened covers and wrapping-cord ties, are among the oldest surviving bound books anywhere and show the technology essentially complete.
nodes.src: Colin Roberts & T.C. Skeat, The Birth of the Codex (1983). The Nag Hammadi bindings: James Robinson, The Nag Hammadi Story (2014); J.M. Robinson, 'The Construction of the Nag Hammadi Codices', in Krause (ed.), Essays on the Nag Hammadi Texts (1975).

nodes.label: Coptic chant and the end of the theatre
nodes.full: Church music replaced public spectacle. The monasteries built a whole discipline of psalmody — chanting the psalter through in weekly cycles — and the Egyptian church developed its own body of hymns and melodic modes for the liturgy, sung by trained cantors and preserved by oral transmission ever since. Meanwhile the mime, the pantomime and the chariot races drew ever fiercer clerical condemnation, and by the seventh century Egypt's classical theatres stood empty.
nodes.src: Coptic chant: Ilona Borsai and the ethnomusicological studies; Marian Robertson-Wilson. The end of the shows: Sofie Remijsen, The End of Greek Athletics in Late Antiquity (2015); Charlotte Roueché on the acclamations.

nodes.label: The last philosophers of Alexandria
nodes.full: The Neoplatonist school survived Hypatia's murder by more than two centuries. Under Ammonius son of Hermeias it reached a working accommodation with the Christian authorities, concentrating on Aristotle and mathematics rather than pagan theology; the last openly pagan head, Olympiodorus, died about 565; and Christian Neoplatonists — Philoponus, Elias, David, Stephanus — carried the tradition to the eve of the Arab conquest, from where its commentaries passed into Syriac and Arabic and shaped medieval philosophy east and west.
nodes.src: Edward Watts, City and School in Late Antique Athens and Alexandria (2006); Richard Sorabji (ed.), Aristotle Transformed: The Ancient Commentators and Their Influence (1990). Olympiodorus and the school's end: L.G. Westerink.

nodes.label: John Philoponus against Aristotle
nodes.full: John Philoponus, a Christian philosopher of Alexandria, mounted the most serious ancient challenge to Aristotelian physics. He argued that the universe was created and not eternal; that a thrown object keeps moving because a force is impressed into it, not because the air pushes it from behind (an anticipation of the idea of impetus, and momentum); and, from dropping weights, that bodies of different mass fall in nearly the same time — a claim Galileo would make again a thousand years later, citing him.
nodes.src: Philoponus, Against Aristotle on the Eternity of the World; Commentary on the Physics. Richard Sorabji (ed.), Philoponus and the Rejection of Aristotelian Science (1987, 2nd ed. 2010).

nodes.label: The Alexandrian medical curriculum
nodes.full: Alexandria's medical school distilled Galen into a teachable canon: a fixed set of sixteen works, studied through summaries and question-and-answer digests (the 'Alexandrian Epitomes') by teachers called iatrosophists. This packaged curriculum was the form in which Greek medicine passed to the Byzantine physicians, and then — as the teaching tradition migrated through Antioch to Baghdad after the conquest — to the Arabic-speaking world, and so to medieval Europe. Alexandria stayed the word for medical authority for another five centuries.
nodes.src: Owsei Temkin, 'Studies on Late Alexandrian Medicine', Bulletin of the History of Medicine 3 (1935). Vivian Nutton, Ancient Medicine (2004) pp.298–309; the 'from Alexandria to Baghdad' tradition, Max Meyerhof (1930).

nodes.label: Cosmas and the Christian world-picture
nodes.full: Cosmas, an Alexandrian merchant who had sailed the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean and later became a monk, wrote the Christian Topography to argue from scripture that the earth is flat and rectangular, shaped like the biblical tabernacle, with the sun circling a great northern mountain — against the pagan doctrine of a spherical earth, which most Christian scholars in fact accepted. The same book is a firsthand source of real value on the trade of Adulis, Socotra and Ceylon and on the Christian communities of India.
nodes.src: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography: Wanda Wolska-Conus's edition (Sources Chrétiennes, 1968–73); J.W. McCrindle's translation (1897). The trade material: Lionel Casson and the Indian Ocean literature.

nodes.label: The Alexandrian computus and the date of Easter
nodes.full: The one science the whole church needed was the calculation of Easter, and it delegated the job to Alexandria, whose astronomers worked out the date from a 19-year lunar cycle and whose patriarch announced it each year in a circular 'Festal Letter'. Rome adopted the Alexandrian method after long resistance; in the sixth century the monk Dionysius Exiguus turned its tables into the 'Anno Domini' year-count now used worldwide. Egyptian calendar mathematics, once the servant of the temple, had become the servant of the church.
nodes.src: The Festal Letters of Athanasius and Cyril. Alden Mosshammer, The Easter Computus and the Origins of the Christian Era (2008); Georges Declercq, Anno Domini: The Origins of the Christian Era (2000).

nodes.label: The grain of Constantinople
nodes.full: From 330 the Egyptian grain tax, once Rome's, was shipped to Constantinople — an annual delivery of the order of eight million artabas that fed the capital's bread dole, carried by a compulsory guild of shippers under close state supervision. It was the material foundation of the eastern empire, and its interruption twice proved catastrophic: the Persian conquest of 619 and the Arab conquest of 642 each cut it off, and Constantinople's population and confidence fell sharply as a result.
nodes.src: Justinian, Edict 13; the Theodosian Code 13–14. Geoffrey Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980); Michael Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985); Jairus Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity (2001).

nodes.label: The estate economy
nodes.full: The great estates ran integrated production units: grain on the best land, vineyards and olive groves on the rest, tenant farmers increasingly bound to their plots, and irrigation machinery maintained as capital equipment. Rents came in both wheat and gold; surplus wine and oil went to market in the towns and abroad. The trend of the period was concentration — land, and the labour on it, gathering into fewer, larger hands, whether of senators, the church, or the crown.
nodes.src: Jairus Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity: Gold, Labour, and Aristocratic Dominance (2001); Peter Sarris, Economy and Society in the Age of Justinian (2006); Todd Hickey, Wine, Wealth, and the State (2012).

nodes.label: The monetised village and the gold solidus
nodes.full: Constantine's gold solidus held its weight and fineness for centuries and became the anchor of the late-antique economy, supported by fractional gold and a shifting copper small change. In Egypt this reached all the way down: village papyri record wages, rents, loans, dowries and tax payments in gold and its fractions, and keep running accounts. The rural economy was more thoroughly and routinely monetised than at almost any point before the modern era.
nodes.src: Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity (2001) is the central study. Roger Bagnall, Currency and Inflation in Fourth Century Egypt (1985); the price data in the Oxyrhynchus and Aphrodito papyri.

nodes.label: The church and monastery as economic engines
nodes.full: The church was a major economic actor. It held enormous estates; its monasteries were workshops that made rope, baskets, mats, linen, wine and bread, ran their own mills and presses, and sold the surplus to the towns; it employed and fed thousands, kept 'poor lists' for regular grain doles, and lent money. The pilgrimage centre at Abu Mina was effectively a religious industrial town. Much of the surplus that had gone to temples now flowed through Christian institutions.
nodes.src: Ewa Wipszycka, Les ressources et les activités économiques des églises en Égypte du IVe au VIIIe siècle (1972); Ariel López, Shenoute of Atripe and the Uses of Poverty (2013); the White Monastery economic documents.

nodes.label: Wine replaces beer
nodes.full: Over late antiquity wine displaced barley beer as the ordinary drink of Egypt — pushed by Christian communion, by the monasteries' own production and trade, and by the estates' commercial vineyards. The vineyards of the Mareotis behind Alexandria and of the Middle Egyptian estates supplied a large export, shipped in the distinctive tall amphorae ('Late Roman Amphora 5/6' and 7) that archaeologists find all round the eastern Mediterranean.
nodes.src: Roberta Tomber and the Late Roman Amphora typologies; Dominic Rathbone, 'The Ancient Economy and Graeco-Roman Egypt', in Criscuolo & Geraci (eds.) (1989). Mareotic wine: Strabo 17.1.14 and the amphora evidence.

nodes.label: Papyrus, linen and glass
nodes.full: Egypt remained the workshop of the Mediterranean for a few key products. It was still the sole source of papyrus, and the Merovingian royal and papal chanceries were writing on Egyptian papyrus into the seventh and even eighth centuries; its fine linen and its glass were exported across the empire; and natron for glassmaking and mummification went out from the Wadi Natrun. These trades outlasted Roman rule and kept Egypt tied into the wider economy under its new masters.
nodes.src: Papyrus in the west: Naphtali Lewis, Papyrus in Classical Antiquity (1974) and its supplement. Glass: Ian Freestone's compositional work locating primary production on the Levantine–Egyptian coast.

nodes.label: Building the churches and the fortified monastery
nodes.full: Christian Egypt sustained a large construction sector. Basilicas — timber-roofed, often with a transept, built of fired brick and re-used pharaonic stone — went up in every town, the grandest at the pilgrim city of Abu Mina and at Hermopolis. The desert monasteries were built like forts, with battered mud-brick or stone walls and a tower keep (qasr) to shelter in during raids; the White Monastery re-used blocks quarried from nearby temples in walls that still stand to their full height.
nodes.src: Peter Grossmann, Christliche Architektur in Ägypten (2002) and Abu Mina I (1989). The White Monastery: Bentley Layton and the recent conservation work.

nodes.label: The saqiya economy
nodes.full: The ox-driven waterwheel — a vertical wheel with a garland of pots, turned through a right-angle pin-and-drum gear by an animal walking a circle — became the backbone of Egyptian farming in late antiquity, its maintenance written into land leases as a standing obligation. It is one of the first large-scale uses of gearing to transmit power, and it let irrigated land carry multiple crops a year, sustaining both the population and the grain shipped to Constantinople.
nodes.src: Thorkild Schiøler, Roman and Islamic Water-Lifting Wheels (1973); Michael Lewis, Millstone and Hammer: The Origins of Water Power (1997) on the gearing. Lease clauses: Jane Rowlandson, Landowners and Tenants in Roman Egypt (1996).

nodes.label: Making books for the church
nodes.full: The demand for scripture, liturgy and theology in both Greek and Coptic supported a book-making craft centred on the monasteries: preparing papyrus and, increasingly, parchment; ruling and copying in a formal book-hand; correcting; and binding folded quires between wooden or leather-covered boards with sewn spines and wrapping ties. The techniques worked out here — the codex, the bound spine, the ruled page — are those of the book ever since.
nodes.src: Colin Roberts & T.C. Skeat, The Birth of the Codex (1983); the Nag Hammadi and White Monastery bindings. Coptic book-hands: Anne Boud'hors and the palaeographical literature.

nodes.label: The fortress of Babylon and the frontier forts
nodes.full: Late Roman military engineering in Egypt centred on the great fortress of Babylon at the head of the Delta — rebuilt by Trajan and strengthened again in late antiquity, with massive round bastions of banded stone and brick, straddling the mouth of the canal to the Red Sea. It was the linchpin of the country's defence and the object whose seven-month siege decided the Arab conquest; two of its towers still stand, embedded in Coptic Cairo.
nodes.src: Peter Sheehan, Babylon of Egypt: The Archaeology of Old Cairo and the Origins of the City (2010). The wider frontier: the Notitia Dignitatum and the surviving Nile fortress-towns.

nodes.label: The Red Sea trade in the Christian era
nodes.full: The India and East Africa trade continued into the Christian centuries but contracted: Berenike and Myos Hormos gave way to Clysma at the head of the Gulf of Suez, and the Christian kingdom of Axum, with its port of Adulis, became the dominant Red Sea power and a partner of Constantinople against Persia. Cosmas, who sailed the route himself around 520, describes its ports, its Christian merchant communities as far as Ceylon, and a trade that was shrinking as the wider ancient economy contracted.
nodes.src: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography, esp. book 2 and 11. Steven Sidebotham, Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route (2011) pp.259–81; Glen Bowersock, The Throne of Adulis (2013).

nodes.label: The conversion of Nubia
nodes.full: In the mid-sixth century rival missions — a Miaphysite one sent by the empress Theodora, a Chalcedonian one by Justinian — competed to convert the three Nubian kingdoms south of Egypt: Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia. Within a generation all three were Christian, and, following Egypt, most of Nubia held to the non-Chalcedonian faith and looked to the Coptic patriarch of Alexandria for its bishops. A distinctively Nubian Christian civilisation, with cathedrals like the painted one at Faras, lasted some eight centuries.
nodes.src: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History 4.6–8, 49–53. William Adams, Nubia: Corridor to Africa (1977); Derek Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002). Faras: Kazimierz Michałowski, Faras (1974).

nodes.label: Egyptian monasticism goes to the world
nodes.full: Egypt's largest export to later history was the monastic ideal. John Cassian, who had spent years among the Egyptian monks, founded a monastery at Marseille around 415 and wrote the Institutes and Conferences that carried desert practice into the Latin west and, through Benedict, into the whole medieval church. The Sayings of the Desert Fathers and the Lives were translated into Latin, Syriac, Armenian, Georgian, Ethiopic and Arabic; wherever Christian monks lived, they were following an Egyptian pattern.
nodes.src: John Cassian, Institutes and Conferences (Boniface Ramsey's translation). Columba Stewart, Cassian the Monk (1998); Derwas Chitty, The Desert a City (1966).

nodes.label: Alexandria and the non-Chalcedonian world
nodes.full: Alexandria was one of the five great patriarchates and, for a century, the most theologically assertive — its bishop styled 'pope' before Rome's claim was fixed, its councils dominant at Nicaea and Ephesus, its rivalry with Constantinople bitter. After Chalcedon the see took on a new role: the head and reference point of the whole non-Chalcedonian communion — the churches of Egypt, Syria, Armenia, and later Ethiopia and Nubia — the Oriental Orthodox family that still exists.
nodes.src: Norman Russell, Cyril of Alexandria (2000); Stephen Davis, The Early Coptic Papacy (2004); W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972).

nodes.label: Pilgrims to the Egyptian holy places
nodes.full: Christian Egypt drew a steady traffic of pilgrims: to the living desert fathers of Nitria and Scetis, to the shrine of St Menas, to Mount Sinai and the bush of Moses, and to the sites where the Holy Family was said to have sheltered. The travellers left accounts — the nun Egeria, the anonymous Piacenza pilgrim, the authors of the Historia Monachorum and the Lausiac History — that are among the best sources for late-antique Egyptian religion and daily life on the road.
nodes.src: Egeria, Itinerarium; the Piacenza Pilgrim; Historia Monachorum in Aegypto; Palladius, Lausiac History. Georgia Frank, The Memory of the Eyes: Pilgrims to Living Saints in Christian Late Antiquity (2000).

nodes.label: The Arab settlement and the dhimma
nodes.full: The conquest began a new exchange, not just a change of ruler. The mass of the population kept its Coptic church under a treaty that levied a land tax and a poll tax (jizya) on non-Muslims and, at first, largely left local society alone; Greek and Coptic stayed the languages of administration for another century; the surplus that had gone to Constantinople now went to Medina, along a re-dug Red Sea canal. Conversion and Arabisation would take centuries — the deep transformation was still ahead.
nodes.src: The conquest-era bilingual papyri (PERF 558 etc.). Petra Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State: The World of a Mid-Eighth-Century Egyptian Official (2013); Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007); Robert Hoyland, In God's Path (2015).

nodes.label: Alexandria the Christian metropolis
nodes.full: Alexandria stayed the empire's second city — perhaps half a million people, the busiest harbours in the Mediterranean, the grain fleet, the mint — but its character changed. The Serapeum was rubble and the Museum decayed; churches and the patriarch's compound dominated the skyline and the politics; the crowd that had rioted over taxes now rioted over creeds. Increasingly Miaphysite and increasingly resentful of Constantinople, the city was a Christian capital half-detached from the empire that owned it.
nodes.src: Christopher Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity: Topography and Social Conflict (1997); Judith McKenzie, The Architecture of Alexandria and Egypt (2007) pp.229–63.

nodes.label: The Nile valley and the monastic desert
nodes.full: The geography of Egypt was rewritten by monks. The deserts on both sides of the valley, empty of settlement for millennia, filled with hermitages and walled monasteries — Nitria, Kellia, Scetis in the north, Pachomian and other houses the length of the south — until contemporaries spoke of 'the desert made a city'. The valley itself split culturally: a Greek-speaking, more Chalcedonian-leaning coast, and a Coptic-speaking interior that was the heartland of the monks and the national church.
nodes.src: Athanasius, Life of Antony 14. James Goehring, 'The Encroaching Desert: Literary Production and Ascetic Space in Early Christian Egypt', Journal of Early Christian Studies 1 (1993); Ewa Wipszycka, Moines et communautés monastiques en Égypte (2009).

nodes.label: The Christian kingdoms of Nubia
nodes.full: South of the cataract stood three kingdoms — Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia — converted in the mid-sixth century and, like Egypt, largely non-Chalcedonian, taking their bishops from the Coptic patriarch of Alexandria. They built brick cathedrals with painted interiors, wrote in Greek, Coptic and their own Old Nubian, and traded gold, ivory and slaves north. This Christian Nubian civilisation, tied to Egypt by faith, would outlast Byzantine Egypt by some seven centuries.
nodes.src: Derek Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002); William Adams, Nubia: Corridor to Africa (1977). Faras cathedral: Kazimierz Michałowski, Faras: Die Kathedrale aus dem Wüstensand (1967).

nodes.label: Plague, cooling and decline
nodes.full: The sixth century brought two linked disasters. A run of huge volcanic eruptions from 536 cooled the northern hemisphere for decades, and in 541 bubonic plague entered the Roman world through the Egyptian port of Pelusium, killing perhaps a third of the population in its first wave and recurring for two centuries. Abandoned villages, shrinking towns and falling tax yields show an Egypt materially poorer and emptier in 641 than it had been in 300 — a weakened country when the Arab armies came.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 2.22–23 (plague at Pelusium). Kyle Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017); Lester Little (ed.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007); Ulf Büntgen et al., 'Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age', Nature Geoscience 9 (2016).

nodes.label: Antony of the Desert
nodes.full: Antony was a Coptic-speaking farmer's son from Middle Egypt who, hearing the gospel read in church, sold his inherited land and withdrew — first to the village edge, then to a desert fort where he lived walled up for twenty years, then to a mountain by the Red Sea. Athanasius made him the archetype of the monk; his own surviving letters reveal a more learned, speculative, Origen-influenced mind than that portrait allows. He is the founder-figure of Christian monasticism worldwide.
nodes.src: Athanasius, Life of Antony. Samuel Rubenson, The Letters of St. Antony: Monasticism and the Making of a Saint (1995).

nodes.label: Shenoute of Atripe
nodes.full: Shenoute ran the White Monastery for something like eighty years as an absolute ruler of several thousand monks and nuns, enforcing his rule with beatings and expulsions and once, by his own account, killing a monk through excessive punishment. He led armed raids on the estates and shrines of the district's pagan gentry, sheltered thousands of refugees from desert raids, defied governors, and wrote the sermons and letters that are the masterpiece of Coptic literature — the fullest, most human portrait of the late-antique holy man in power.
nodes.src: Stephen Emmel, Shenoute's Literary Corpus (2004); Ariel López, Shenoute of Atripe and the Uses of Poverty (2013); Caroline Schroeder, Monastic Bodies: Discipline and Salvation in Shenoute of Atripe (2007).

nodes.label: Hypatia of Alexandria
nodes.full: Hypatia, daughter and colleague of the mathematician Theon, led the Neoplatonist school of Alexandria, taught philosophy publicly, and wrote commentaries on the algebra of Diophantus, the conics of Apollonius and the astronomy of Ptolemy; she is credited with helping design an astrolabe and a hydrometer. Her pupil Synesius, later a bishop, wrote her devoted letters. She was murdered by a Christian mob in 415, caught between the prefect and the patriarch — an emblem ever since of learning destroyed by fanaticism.
nodes.src: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 7.15; Synesius, Letters 10, 15, 16, 81, 124. Maria Dzielska, Hypatia of Alexandria (1995); Edward Watts, Hypatia: The Life and Legend of an Ancient Philosopher (2017).

nodes.label: The house of Apion
nodes.full: The Apiones were among the richest families of the eastern empire — senators, consuls and praetorian prefects at Constantinople, landlords of tens of thousands of hectares around Oxyrhynchus. Their estate archive lets a late-Roman great house be reconstructed in extraordinary detail: its accounts and payrolls, its private army and prison, its churches and monasteries, its collection of the imperial taxes, and the thousands of tenants, workers and clients who depended on it. The family disappears from the record with the Persian conquest.
nodes.src: E.R. Hardy, The Large Estates of Byzantine Egypt (1931); Todd Hickey, Wine, Wealth, and the State in Late Antique Egypt: The House of Apion at Oxyrhynchus (2012); Peter Sarris, Economy and Society in the Age of Justinian (2006).

nodes.label: Dioscorus of Aphrodito
nodes.full: Dioscorus was the leading man of an Upper Egyptian village: a landowner, a lawyer, the notary who drew up his neighbours' contracts, and an ambitious composer of Greek verse who travelled to Constantinople to defend Aphrodito's right to pay its taxes directly to the state. His archive — legal documents, petitions against the local strongman, drafts of his own laboured poems — is a self-portrait of a provincial notable in the last generation of Byzantine Egypt.
nodes.src: Leslie MacCoull, Dioscorus of Aphrodito: His Work and His World (1988); Jean-Luc Fournet (ed.), Les archives de Dioscore d'Aphrodité cent ans après leur découverte (2008).

nodes.label: The women of Christian Egypt
nodes.full: Christianity opened new roles and closed others for Egyptian women. Female ascetics — the 'ammas' whose sayings sit beside the fathers' in the desert collections, the thousands of nuns in the Pachomian and White Monastery communities, the wealthy Roman aristocrat Melania the Younger who came to liquidate her fortune among the monks — chose a life outside marriage and household. The ordinary women of the papyri, meanwhile, went on owning land, lending money and going to court in a society that was steadily rewriting the rules around them.
nodes.src: The Sayings of Amma Syncletica, Amma Sarah, Amma Theodora. Gerontius, Life of Melania the Younger. Rebecca Krawiec, Shenoute and the Women of the White Monastery (2002); Susanna Elm, Virgins of God (1994).

nodes.label: Cyrus, Benjamin, and the men at the turn
nodes.full: The conquest is framed by two rival patriarchs of Alexandria. Cyrus 'the Caucasian', a Chalcedonian sent by Heraclius to force church union, ran a hard persecution of the Copts, then negotiated the surrender of Egypt to 'Amr — recalled in disgrace, tried, sent back, and dead within weeks of the treaty he signed. Benjamin, the Coptic patriarch he had driven into hiding for thirteen years, returned under Arab safe-conduct to rebuild his church. One man's world ended; the other's began.
nodes.src: John of Nikiou, ch.116–21; the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria. Phil Booth, 'The Muslim Conquest of Egypt Reconsidered', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013) and 'The Last Years of Cyrus', TM 20/1 (2016).
